tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — DANGLING OAT SPIKELETS
tiles.details: Begin with the TWO archived Texas in-situ Avena fatua photos (panels 4–5): trace each open, often nodding, branched panicle to the pendent spikelets. Panel 0 adds an older source-identified flowering view. None exposes connected roots or proves the mature floret callus. A 7–40 cm panicle and 2–3-flowered large spikelets are published traits, not independently measured from these photographs. Contrast the unbranched spikes of Hordeum and Secale.
tiles.short: Loose, nodding branched panicle with large hanging 2–3-flowered spikelets; not a barley or rye spike.
tiles.status: REAL TEXAS HABIT PHOTOS — RIPE FLORET STILL REQUIRED

tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTS AND TRUE LEAF COLLAR
tiles.details: Panel 1 is a physically archived Matt Lavin true INNER membranous ligule at the blade–sheath junction; its nearby finger is not a millimeter ruler. The 4–6 mm membrane and lack of auricles are published descriptions, not demonstrated measurements. A same-plant Texas rooted crown, opened collar and millimeter scale remain needed.
tiles.short: Cool-season fibrous-rooted annual; 4–6 mm acute membranous ligule; auricles absent.
tiles.status: ACTUAL INNER LIGULE PHOTO — CALIBRATED TEXAS SAME-PLANT VIEW MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · TWO LARGE GLUMES ENCLOSE THE FLORETS
tiles.details: Panel 2 is a physically archived opened A. fatua spikelet with actual papery outer glumes, inner florets and stout awn. At 10–20× measure one ripe 18–32 mm spikelet and two separately exposed 18–32 mm, commonly 9–11-veined glumes; count 2–3 florets inside ONE spikelet. The photograph is not calibrated and does not prove those vein counts. Published measurements are not pixel measurements.
tiles.short: Mature spikelet 18–32 mm; 2(–3) florets; two subequal 18–32 mm, usually 9–11-veined glumes.
tiles.status: PARTIAL MACRO — SEPARATED MEASURED GLUMES MISSING

tiles.heading: 04 · HAIRY LEMMA, DORSAL BENT AWN AND CALLUS
tiles.details: Panel 3 is a physically archived Matt Lavin detached floret with genuine basal hairs and a twisted, knee-bent awn. Published fertile lemma length is about 14–22 mm and awn about 23–42 mm, dorsally inserted near the middle third; the gallery cannot yet measure or independently pinpoint that attachment or a natural shattering scar. Photograph the ripe detached floret at 10–20× with a ruler and a clear callus/rachilla scar.
tiles.short: Fertile lemma 14–22 mm; dorsal twisted/knee-bent awn 23–42 mm, inserted near lemma middle third.
tiles.status: ACTUAL MACRO — AWN ORIGIN/CALLUS SCAR NEED SCALE

tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Panels 6 and 7 are EXPLICITLY OTHER-SPECIES photographs: Avena barbata (slender oat) spikelet and cultivated A. sativa whole plant. Panels 2–3 are genuine A. fatua anatomy. Compare same-stage ripe spikelets, awn insertion, callus hairs and natural disarticulation; A. sativa and A. fatua can overlap, and A. barbata must not be mislabeled wild oat. Bromus japonicus has smaller many-flowered spikelets with near-tip lemma awns; Hordeum and Secale bear unbranched spikes. If ripe floret characters remain unresolved, record Avena sp.
tiles.short: Cultivated oat can mimic wild oat; Japanese brome has tip-origin lemma awns.
tiles.status: REAL TWO-SPECIES COMPARISONS — MATCHED RIPE FLORETS STILL NEEDED

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE AND EXACT HANDOFF
tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: a connected rooted Texas A. fatua annual with intact panicle; opened 4–6 mm true inner ligule with physical 1-mm ruler; mature 2–3-flowered spikelet with separated countable-vein glumes and scale; detached ripe 14–22 mm lemma, 23–42 mm dorsal awn insertion, hairy callus and natural disarticulation scar at 10–20×; matched mature A. barbata and A. sativa florets at the same scale. NEEDS_SITE_QA: verify 8 local JPEGs, 6 own-species and 2 other-species panels, 4 existing gross markers, exact photographer/CC BY-NC/BY-SA/BY/public-domain permissions, modification/ShareAlike notices, EXIF/GPS policy, public gallery labels and mobile rendering. No site deployment asserted.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — real anatomical photos exist; scaled dissection and live-site QA remain.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: INTRODUCED wild oat: a loose, open, often dangling panicle with large narrow hanging multi-flowered spikelets, each commonly with long knee-bent/twisted awns. Check callus hairs, two glumes and individual fertile lemma awn under a lens. Its drooping spikelet looks like oats, but cannot identify A. fatua versus cultivated oats without mature florets.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Panel 1 is a physically archived Matt Lavin true INNER membranous ligule at the blade–sheath junction; its nearby finger is not a millimeter ruler. The 4–6 mm membrane and lack of auricles are published descriptions, not demonstrated measurements. A same-plant Texas rooted crown, opened collar and millimeter scale remain needed.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Begin with the TWO archived Texas in-situ Avena fatua photos (panels 4–5): trace each open, often nodding, branched panicle to the pendent spikelets. Panel 0 adds an older source-identified flowering view. None exposes connected roots or proves the mature floret callus. A 7–40 cm panicle and 2–3-flowered large spikelets are published traits, not independently measured from these photographs. Contrast the unbranched spikes of Hordeum and Secale.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Compare cultivated Avena sativa (oat)—often less disarticulation/hairiness and fewer conspicuous twisted awns. Hordeum and Secale have compact central spikes rather than a loose dangling oat panicle. Treat as introduced, not a native Hays County grass.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: LOOK-ALIKE · slender oat (*Avena barbata*), photographed spikelet and glumes
panels.caption: SLENDER / BEARDED OAT (Avena barbata), photographed by Harry Rose. Its spikelets carry long glumes and awned florets, broadly resembling wild oat. Compare opened mature florets and especially lemma-tip teeth under a millimeter ruler: A. barbata generally has longer bifid lemma teeth than A. fatua. No identification by simply counting the two long glumes.
panels.creator: Harry Rose
